content_voiceover: This figure walks through the mechanism of paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria, or PCH. It starts with Donath-Landsteiner antibodies, which are produced after a trigger, classically a viral upper respiratory infection in children. In the periphery, where temperatures drop below thirty-seven degrees, these IgG antibodies bind to the P antigen on the red cell surface. This is the key point for boards. The Donath-Landsteiner antibody is a biphasic hemolysin. It attaches to red cells in the cold and fixes complement, specifically C3d, while still cold. Then, as blood returns to the warmer core circulation at thirty-seven degrees, the complement cascade completes and the red cells lyse right there in the vessel. So you get intravascular hemolysis triggered by a cold-to-warm cycle, even though the antibody itself doesn't cause visible agglutination like a typical cold agglutinin. Remember this pattern, cold binding, warm lysis, that's the biphasic hallmark of PCH.
keypoints: Donath-Landsteiner antibody is a biphasic IgG hemolysin
Binds P antigen on RBCs in the cold, fixes complement C3d
Complement completes and lyses RBCs when warmed to 37 degrees C
Causes intravascular hemolysis, classic post-viral URI trigger in children
